structure.title: Books I–II · From a household to a constitution
structure.text: Aristotle begins with forms of rule inside a household and asks what changes when households form a city. He measures proposed arrangements, including Plato's common guardianship, against the practical demands of belonging, property and care.

structure.title: Book III · Who counts as a citizen?
structure.text: Residence alone cannot settle membership. Taking part in judgment and office supplies a more political answer, which immediately raises a difficulty. The person entitled to rule in a democracy may have no such standing in an oligarchy.

structure.title: Books IV–VI · Constitutions that actually have to survive
structure.text: Combinations of wealth, numbers, offices and methods of election generate more varieties of government than a simple list of regime names suggests. Aristotle becomes especially attentive to grievances that can turn an ordinary dispute into an attempt to change the whole settlement.

structure.title: Books VII–VIII · What should a city make possible?
structure.text: The inquiry returns to the best life with questions about population, place, leisure and schooling. Music receives political attention because the uses people make of free time help determine what all their work was for.

people.name: The citizen
people.role: A participant in ruling and being ruled
people.text: Aristotle distinguishes excellence as a member of a particular constitution from excellence as a human being. The two measures can diverge sharply when the regime rewards conduct a good person has reason to question.

people.name: Rich and poor
people.text: One side sees inequality of wealth as a title to unequal power. The other sees equality of free birth as a title to equal shares. Each starts from a relevant difference and risks making it the whole measure.

people.name: The legislator
people.role: A designer working with available materials
people.text: A constitution attractive in the abstract may be impossible to sustain in a particular city. To advise a legislator, Aristotle needs an account both of desirable ends and of the kind of change the citizens can bear.

context.title: Freedom rests on excluded labour
context.text: Women, enslaved people and many workers figure in the account without receiving equal political standing. Aristotle's defence of supposedly natural slavery is a contested claim within his own discussion. The distribution of leisure and political voice depends on these exclusions.

context.title: A Greek city is a political community
context.text: The city includes fields, households and the institutions through which citizens deliberate. If one imagines only an urban centre, Aristotle's questions about land, military service and who grows food can look oddly detached from his subject.

notice.text: Count the small devices that decide who attends.
notice.why: Paying poorer citizens to serve or fining wealthier citizens for absence can alter an assembly without changing its declared powers. Political balance sometimes turns on who can afford an afternoon away.

notice.text: Listen for the question of whose good is served.
notice.why: The count of rulers by itself cannot distinguish king from tyrant. Asking whose advantage guides their decisions changes the classification even when the number of people in office stays exactly the same.

opening: The rich say their property entitles them to rule; the poor say their numbers do. Both can make a claim about justice, and both have reasons to confuse the city's good with their own advantage. Aristotle examines constitutions as arrangements made by people who want different things from living together. His investigation includes arguments about slavery and exclusion that demand resistance, alongside a persistent practical question: how can a community govern itself without letting one group's victory become everybody else's insecurity?
